Grandma Joan's Victoria Sponge
225g butter, softened
225g caster sugar
4 large eggs
225g self-raising flour
1 tsp baking powder
2 tbsp milk
Heat oven to 180°C (160°C fan), gas mark 4. Grease and line two 20cm tins.
Beat everything together until smooth, divide between the tins and bake for 20–25 minutes.
Sandwich with raspberry jam and dust with icing sugar.

Cheese Scones (makes 8)
225g self-raising flour
55g cold butter, cubed
85g mature Cheddar, grated
1/2 tsp mustard powder
150ml milk, plus extra to glaze
Rub the butter into the flour, stir in the cheese and mustard, then add milk to make a soft dough. Pat out to 2cm thick, cut with a 6cm cutter, glaze and bake at 220°C for 12–15 min.

Aunt Dot's Cornbread
1 cup cornmeal
1 cup all-purpose flour
1/4 cup sugar
1 tbsp baking powder
1 tsp salt
1 cup buttermilk
1/3 cup melted butter
1 egg
Preheat oven to 400°F. Mix the dry ingredients, whisk in the wet, pour into a greased 8-inch square pan and bake 20 to 25 minutes until golden.

Brackenford Show Green Tomato Chutney
1.5kg green tomatoes, chopped
500g onions, chopped
250g sultanas
400g soft brown sugar
600ml malt vinegar
1 1/2 tsp ground ginger
Put everything in a large pan and simmer gently for 2 1/2 hours, stirring often, until thick. Pot into hot sterilised jars and seal. Keeps 12 months.

Shepherd's Pie (serves 4–6)
1 tbsp oil
500g lamb mince
1 onion and 2 carrots, finely diced
2 tbsp tomato purée
400ml lamb stock
1 tbsp Worcestershire sauce
900g potatoes, mashed with 50g butter
Brown the mince, add the veg and soften for 10 min. Stir in the purée, stock and Worcestershire sauce and simmer for 20 min. Top with the mash and bake at 200°C for 25–30 minutes.

Lunchbox Flapjacks (cuts into 16)
250g porridge oats
125g butter
125g light brown sugar
3 tbsp golden syrup
Pinch of salt

THE CORN EXCHANGE
The Corn Exchange was built in 1857 at a cost of £3,240, raised largely by subscription among the town's farmers and merchants. Its great hall, 96 feet long, could hold 700 people, and for more than eighty years it rang every Thursday with the bargaining of corn dealers.
After the last grain sale in 1938 the building served as a drill hall, a cinema and, from 1974, the town's main venue for concerts and plays.

St Aldric's Church
The church is mostly 14th-century, though the north doorway, with its zigzag carving, survives from a Norman building of about 1140. The tower, 112ft high, was added in 1462 and holds a ring of 8 bells, the heaviest weighing 18 cwt.
Inside, look for the medieval wall painting of St Christopher opposite the south door and the brass of Thomas Wolley, wool merchant, d. 1503.
Open daily 9am–5pm.

Descaling your kettle
In hard water areas such as Brackenford, descale every 4 to 6 weeks.
1. Fill the kettle with 500ml of water and 500ml of white vinegar.

3. Empty, rinse three times and boil once with clean water before use.

The Great Flood of 1947
On 16 March 1947 the River Wenn rose 9ft 6in above its normal level, the highest ever recorded at the town bridge. Water stood 3 feet deep in Mill Lane and Bridge Street, and 140 households had to be rehoused for up to six weeks.
A brass plate on the wall of the Bridge Inn still marks the height of the water.

In mild areas, sow 'Aquadulce' type broad beans outdoors in late October or November for an early crop the following June. Elsewhere, sow from February to April.
